metadata.title: Competition or cooperation: Which is better for students’ academic performance? A multi‑level analysis across cultures based on PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 secondary microdata with a two-stage stratified sampling design (schools, then students within schools). The authors report that population means in Table 1 are calculated using official PISA 2018 survey weights, but the multilevel regression estimation is described as being run in Stata 18.0 with country dummies and imputation dummies; the manuscript does not explicitly state the exact weight variable(s) used in the HLM estimation. For missing data, the authors impute using school- and country-level means and include imputation dummies, and they conduct robustness checks using OLS with standard errors estimated using Fay’s variant of BRR to account for the hierarchical structure. Because the paper does not clearly document whether complex survey weights (and which weight variable) were applied in the main HLM models, readers should treat the estimates as primarily model-based associations rather than fully design-weighted population inferences.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 student microdata for 15-year-olds in mathematics, science, and reading. The analytic sample includes up to 576,142 students from 20,631 schools across 76 countries/economies, excluding Canada, Cyprus, and Vietnam due to missing or invalid information for the outcome or primary independent variables. The study then groups the remaining countries/economies into eight cultural regions (Schwartz, 2009) for multilevel analyses across cultures. For missing values in predictors/covariates, the authors impute using school-level means and country-level means and add imputation dummies for each variable with missing values; robustness checks are run using the original non-imputed dataset.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (10 plausible values, student-level; multilevel across 76 countries/economies)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level hierarchical regression (null vs full). ICC (null): 49.4%. Full model fixed effects: student perceived competition β = -1.588 (p < .01); student perceived cooperation β = 0.971 (p < .001); school competition β = 3.299 (p < .001); school cooperation β = 21.312 (p < .001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading the study leveraged student perceived competition, student perceived cooperation, school competition, and school cooperation to predict reading achievement (PVs), finding that student perceived competition was negatively associated with reading while both student and especially school cooperation were positively associated. This indicates that strengthening cooperative school climates may yield larger reading gains than relying on competitive messaging, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (10 plausible values, student-level; multilevel across 76 countries/economies)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level hierarchical regression (null vs full). ICC (null): 51.8%. Full model fixed effects: student perceived competition β = -0.648 (p < .001); student perceived cooperation β = 1.812 (p < .001); school competition β = 4.962 (p < .001); school cooperation β = 19.744 (p < .001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics the study leveraged student perceived competition, student perceived cooperation, school competition, and school cooperation to predict mathematics achievement (PVs), finding that student perceived competition was negatively associated with mathematics while student cooperation and both school-level constructs were positively associated—particularly school cooperation. This indicates that policies promoting cooperative learning structures at the school level may be more effective for mathematics improvement than emphasizing competition, while acknowledging that reverse causality may still bias associations.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Science (10 plausible values, student-level; multilevel across 76 countries/economies)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level hierarchical regression (null vs full). ICC (null): 49.4%. Full model fixed effects: student perceived competition β = -0.940 (p < .001); student perceived cooperation β = 1.196 (p < .001); school competition β = 4.031 (p < .001); school cooperation β = 19.321 (p < .001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Science the study leveraged student perceived competition, student perceived cooperation, school competition, and school cooperation to predict science achievement (PVs), finding that student perceived competition was negatively associated with science while cooperation at both student and school levels was positively associated, with school cooperation showing the strongest relationship. This indicates that fostering cooperative school climates may support science learning outcomes across diverse contexts, though causal claims cannot be made from cross-sectional PISA perceptions.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-olds across 76 countries/economies (after excluding Canada, Cyprus, and Vietnam) to examine how student-perceived and school-level competition and cooperation relate to achievement in reading, mathematics, and science. Outcomes are PISA plausible values: 10 PVs per subject are analyzed jointly using Stata’s pv command, and the authors estimate two-level hierarchical regression models to account for the nested student–school structure (ICC around 49–52% in the null models). In the pooled models, student perceived competition is consistently negatively associated with achievement (e.g., reading β = −1.588, p < .01), while student perceived cooperation is positive (reading β = 0.971, p < .001) and school cooperation shows the strongest positive associations (reading β = 21.312, p < .001; mathematics β = 19.744, p < .001; science β = 19.321, p < .001). Missing data are imputed using school- and country-level means with imputation dummies, and robustness checks use non-imputed data with OLS standard errors via Fay’s BRR. Because the design is cross-sectional and student perceptions may reflect reverse causality, the results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.
